metadata.title: The effects of ICT-based social media on adolescents' digital reading performance: A longitudinal study of PISA 2009, PISA 2012, PISA 2015 and PISA 2018

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA microdata from four cycles (2009, 2012, 2015, 2018) and applies normalized student weights throughout the multilevel analyses to obtain unbiased estimates under PISA’s complex sampling design. The authors fit random-intercept fixed-slope hierarchical linear models (HLM) separately for each cycle, explicitly accounting for the nested student–school–country structure. Plausible values for digital reading performance are handled via multiple imputation and Rubin’s rules, with pooled estimates produced by the HLM software. The manuscript does not report a specific weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it states that normalized student weights were used; replicate weights are not mentioned.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample includes, for each PISA cycle (2009, 2012, 2015, 2018), only countries/regions that participated in the computer-based reading assessment and completed the student questionnaire, school questionnaire, and ICT familiarity questionnaire. Countries/regions with complete missing data on required variables were excluded, yielding 57 countries/regions and 767,511 students across 27,943 schools. The dependent variable is PISA computer-based reading performance, operationalized using PISA-provided plausible values (5 PVs in 2009/2012; 10 PVs in 2015/2018). Missing questionnaire/ICT variables were handled via multiple imputation (predictive mean matching) rather than listwise deletion.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical linear model (random intercept, fixed slopes). Reported fixed-effect estimates (Gamma) with t-tests and p-values; no predictive ML metrics (e.g., AUC/RMSE) reported. Example significant effects: USEREC1_2 Gamma=15.21 (p<0.001), USEREC1_3 Gamma=20.91 (p<0.001), USEREC1_4 Gamma=26.46 (p<0.001); USEREC2_2 Gamma=−2.75 (p=0.041); USEREC2_3 Gamma=−2.34 (p=0.017); USESCH1_2 Gamma=−19.54 (p<0.001); ESCS Gamma=19.76 (p<0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009 digital reading performance the study leveraged recreational email use, recreational chatting use, recreational browsing fun use, recreational online news use, and recreational online games use to predict students’ digital reading performance (PVs), finding that recreational email, browsing for fun, and reading online news were associated with higher performance while recreational online games were associated with lower performance. This indicates that encouraging specific text-based social media activities outside school may support digital reading skills, while gaming via social networks may require tighter guidance to avoid distraction.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical linear model (random intercept, fixed slopes). Reported fixed-effect estimates (Gamma) with t-tests and p-values; no predictive ML metrics reported. Example significant effects: USEREC1_2 Gamma=11.46 (p<0.001), USEREC1_3 Gamma=17.35 (p<0.001), USEREC1_4 Gamma=19.57 (p<0.001); USEREC2_2 Gamma=−4.85 (p<0.001), USEREC2_3 Gamma=−4.37 (p<0.001); USEREC3_2 Gamma=−4.78 (p=0.004); USEACA1_2 Gamma=−5.92 (p<0.001); USEACA2_2 Gamma=2.43 (p=0.001); USESCH1_2 Gamma=−25.39 (p<0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 digital reading performance the study leveraged recreational email use, recreational chatting use, recreational social network use, academic social network use (students), and academic email use (teachers) to predict students’ digital reading performance (PVs), finding that email and some recreational online activities were positively associated with performance while chatting and several academic communication uses were negatively associated. This indicates that policy and school guidance should differentiate between social media purposes (recreational vs academic) and communication targets (peers vs teachers) rather than treating social media use as uniformly beneficial or harmful.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical linear model (random intercept, fixed slopes). Reported fixed-effect estimates (Gamma) with t-tests and p-values; no predictive ML metrics reported. Example significant effects: USEREC1_2 Gamma=12.05 (p<0.001), USEREC1_3 Gamma=17.55 (p<0.001), USEREC1_4 Gamma=19.19 (p<0.001); USEREC3_2 Gamma=−5.97 (p<0.001) and USEREC3_3 Gamma=−0.24 (p=0.799) (mixed); USEACA3_2 Gamma=3.45 (p<0.001) and USEACA3_3 Gamma=10.16 (p<0.001); ATT_2 Gamma=18.04 (p<0.001), ATT_3 Gamma=24.16 (p<0.001), ATT_4 Gamma=29.83 (p<0.001); M_ATT_4 Gamma=33.83 (p=0.046).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 digital reading performance the study leveraged recreational email use, recreational social network use, academic social network use (students), school median perceived usefulness, and perceived usefulness of social media to predict students’ digital reading performance (PVs), finding that perceived usefulness of social media was strongly and positively associated with digital reading while peer-focused academic social networking also showed positive effects. This indicates that interventions that build students’ beliefs about the usefulness of social media for learning may be a scalable lever for improving digital reading outcomes, especially when paired with peer-collaboration norms.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical linear model (random intercept, fixed slopes). Reported fixed-effect estimates (Gamma) with t-tests and p-values; no predictive ML metrics reported. Example significant effects: USEREC1_2 Gamma=13.38 (p<0.001), USEREC1_3 Gamma=17.68 (p<0.001), USEREC1_4 Gamma=19.32 (p<0.001); USEREC2_2 Gamma=−6.45 (p<0.001) and USEREC2_3 Gamma=−2.31 (p=0.003); USEREC3_4 Gamma=0.98 (p=0.160) and USEREC3_5 Gamma=−2.50 (p<0.001) (generally negative at higher frequencies); USEACA3_4 Gamma=16.65 (p<0.001) and USEACA3_5 Gamma=11.05 (p<0.001); USEACA4_2 Gamma=−15.71 (p<0.001) and USEACA4_3 Gamma=−26.11 (p<0.001); ATT_2 Gamma=16.23 (p<0.001), ATT_3 Gamma=24.56 (p<0.001), ATT_4 Gamma=30.55 (p<0.001); M_ATT_4 Gamma=27.23 (p=0.114).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 digital reading performance the study leveraged recreational email use, recreational social network use, academic social network use (students), academic social network use (teachers), and perceived usefulness of social media to predict students’ digital reading performance (PVs), finding that perceived usefulness remained significantly positive while teacher-focused academic social networking was consistently negative and peer-focused academic social networking was positive. This indicates that digital reading improvement strategies should promote peer-mediated, purpose-driven social media use and explicitly caution against teacher-mediated communication patterns that may distract or reduce effective reading engagement.

data.outcome_summary: This longitudinal study analyzes PISA computer-based reading performance for 15-year-olds across four cycles (2009, 2012, 2015, 2018), covering 767,511 students from 57 participating countries/regions. The dependent variable is PISA-provided plausible values (5 PVs in 2009/2012; 10 PVs in 2015/2018), combined with multiple imputation for missing questionnaire data (predictive mean matching) and pooled using Rubin’s rules. The authors fit hierarchical linear models (random intercept, fixed slopes) to account for the nested student–school–country structure and report fixed-effect estimates (Gamma) with t-tests and p-values; no predictive ML metrics (AUC/RMSE) are reported because the analysis is not ML-based. Across cycles, recreational email, browsing for fun, and reading online news tend to be positive, while chatting and social-network gaming are often negative; perceived usefulness of social media is consistently positive. Limitations include reliance on frequency-based ICT/social media measures, cycle-specific questionnaire revisions, and the observational nature of PISA (no causal identification).
